title: Measuring Risk and Return
intro: Return is easy to measure; risk is not. Risk is the chance of not getting what you need when you need it, and no single number captures it. This page covers the standard measures (volatility, drawdown, the Sharpe and Sortino ratios, correlation, value at risk), what each one misses, and why market returns have fatter tails than the bell curve suggests.

blocks.text: Expected return and volatility

The expected return $E[R]$ is the probability-weighted average of possible returns. Volatility is the standard deviation $\sigma$ of returns, the typical size of the swing around the average. For a sample of $n$ periodic returns $r_t$ with mean $\bar r$:

If returns are independent from period to period, variance grows with time, so volatility grows with its square root: $\sigma_{year} = \sigma_{month}\sqrt{12} = \sigma_{day}\sqrt{252}$ (252 trading days). Broad stock markets have had yearly volatility around 15 to 20%, high-grade bond indexes around 4 to 7%, individual stocks often 25 to 50%, and bitcoin 60 to 80%.

Under a normal distribution about two-thirds of years fall within one $\sigma$ of the mean and 95% within two. For a stock market with an 8% expected return and 16% volatility, that means a typical range of −8% to +24%, and a year worse than −24% about one time in forty (in practice somewhat more often; see fat tails below).
Risk shrinks with time, but not the way people think

The *average* yearly return over $T$ years has a standard deviation of $\sigma/\sqrt{T}$, so averages become more predictable over long horizons, and the chance that stocks trail cash over 20 years is much smaller than over one. But the spread of *total wealth* keeps widening with time, and the bad outcomes, though rarer, are larger. Long horizons make stocks more attractive, not risk-free. Japan's Nikkei took about 34 years to regain its 1989 peak in price terms.
Drawdowns

The drawdown is the fall from the previous peak; the maximum drawdown is the worst such fall over a period. It measures what investors actually feel. The S&P 500's worst drawdowns: about −86% from 1929 to 1932, −48% in 1973-74, −49% in 2000-02, −57% in 2007-09, −34% in early 2020. A 60/40 stock and bond portfolio fell about a third in 2008-09. Ask of any strategy: what was its worst drawdown, how long did recovery take, and could I have held on?

blocks.caption: A 20% loss needs 25% to recover; 50% needs 100%; 80% needs 400%.

blocks.text: Risk-adjusted return

items: Sharpe ratio (William Sharpe, 1966): excess return over the risk-free rate per unit of volatility, $S = (E[R] - r_f)/\sigma$. Broad stock markets have long-run Sharpe ratios around 0.3 to 0.5. A strategy claiming a Sharpe ratio above 2 for years deserves suspicion (or a very careful look at its tail risk).
Sortino ratio: the same with downside deviation (counting only returns below a target) in place of volatility, so upside swings aren't penalized.
Calmar ratio: yearly return / maximum drawdown.
Information ratio: active return over a benchmark divided by tracking error (the volatility of that active return). The yardstick for active managers.

Alpha and beta: from a regression of the asset's excess returns on the market's, $R_i - r_f = \alpha + \beta(R_m - r_f) + \varepsilon$. Beta is market sensitivity; alpha is return not explained by it (see Portfolio Theory).

blocks.text: Sharpe ratios computed from monthly data are scaled to yearly by $\sqrt{12}$. They assume returns are roughly normal and independent: strategies that sell insurance (short options, carry trades) show high Sharpe ratios until the rare crash, and illiquid assets with smoothed prices show artificially low volatility.
Correlation and covariance

Correlation $\rho$ between two assets runs from −1 (always move opposite) through 0 (unrelated) to +1 (move together). Covariance is $\text{cov}(A, B) = \rho\,\sigma_A\sigma_B$. Correlation is what makes diversification work: the volatility of a mix depends on how its parts move together, not just on their individual volatilities (see Portfolio Theory). Two cautions: correlations are unstable, and they tend to rise in crises ('in a crash, all correlations go to one'), just when diversification is needed most; and correlation measures only linear co-movement on average, not whether two assets crash together.
Fat tails and skew

Real market returns are not normal. Daily stock returns show fat tails (excess kurtosis): extreme days happen far more often than the bell curve allows. On 19 October 1987 the Dow fell 22.6% in a day, a move that a normal model with typical volatility would put at more than 20 standard deviations, essentially impossible. Returns also show negative skew: big falls are more common than equally big rises. And volatility clusters: calm periods and turbulent periods each persist, which ARCH and GARCH models (Engle, Bollerslev) capture.

Benoit Mandelbrot noticed fat tails in cotton prices in the 1960s; Nassim Taleb popularized the point that rare, extreme 'black swan' events dominate long-run outcomes. The practical lesson: don't size positions or leverage as if the normal distribution were true, and stress-test against historical crashes, not only against standard deviations.
Value at risk and expected shortfall

Value at risk (VaR) answers: what loss will not be exceeded with a given confidence over a given period? A one-day 99% VaR of \$1 million means losses should exceed \$1 million on about one day in a hundred. Under normality, $VaR_{\alpha} \approx (z_{\alpha}\sigma - \mu)\times V$ with $z_{0.99} = 2.33$ and $z_{0.95} = 1.645$. VaR says nothing about *how bad* those worst days are, and fat tails make the normal version too optimistic. Expected shortfall (CVaR), the average loss on the days beyond VaR, addresses that and is now preferred by bank regulators.
Risks numbers miss

items: Shortfall risk: not reaching a goal (retirement income, a house deposit). Often the risk that matters most for individuals, and cash can be the riskiest asset for a long goal.
Liquidity risk: needing to sell when no one wants to buy.
Leverage and margin risk: being forced to sell at the bottom.
Concentration risk: too much in one stock (often an employer's: Enron employees held much of their 401(k)s in Enron stock), one sector or one country.
Counterparty and fraud risk: the institution holding your money failing or lying (Madoff, FTX).
Behavioral risk: selling in a panic. The best measure of your risk tolerance is what you did in the last crash.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Annualizing
blocks.text: A fund's monthly returns have a standard deviation of 4.5%. What is its yearly volatility? If its average excess return is 0.6% a month, what is its yearly Sharpe ratio?

blocks.title: Recovering from a loss
blocks.text: A portfolio falls 35%. What return does it need to get back to its peak? At 7% a year, roughly how long will that take?

blocks.title: VaR
blocks.text: A \$500,000 portfolio has daily volatility of 1.2% and roughly zero daily mean. Under normality, what is its one-day 95% VaR? Why might the real figure be worse?
solution: $VaR \approx 1.645 \times 0.012 \times 500000 \approx \$9{,}870$. Real returns have fat tails and volatility clusters, so on bad days losses beyond this level are bigger and more frequent than the normal model says; expected shortfall would be a better gauge.
